sentences: The degree of idealization also predicts the degree of demonization for me.
I don’t mean it as a clinical diagnosis, but I do use it almost like one in my own life.
If a woman says, “You’re such a great guy.
Of course you have flaws like anyone, but I love you,” that sounds healthy.
If she says, “You’re perfect, I can’t find any flaw,” I’m already running.
When the BPD splitting happens, she can go from worshipping me to hating me, first in private and then in front of everybody.
Suddenly she can find plenty of flaws, and all of them become evidence I was faking it all along.
Sometimes she ends up accusing me of thinking I’m perfect, when she’s the one who used to say I was.

haiku: The rhythm mostly varies and stays conversational, with short sentences and a first-person voice that stays inside the experience, so the machine-like signal is weak. The one habit that reads arranged is the paragraph's tendency to close on a tidy reversal.
sonnet: The paragraph is built as a thesis, then an illustration, then an ironic reversal, with every sentence resolving into a neat balanced point and no loose or messy edges. The rhythm is even and the generalized "she" is an archetype, not a particular person, though the first-person stance keeps it from being fully generic.
